# maystash

> Personal site of May — long-form, reproducible writing on AI agents, second brains
> (persistent AI memory systems), security, and building products from zero.
> Every article is a complete blueprint: frameworks, templates, and copy-paste starter kits.
> Plain-markdown source, no paywall, no gating.

## Posts

- [The AI Memory Everyone's Building Is a Diary. Here's How to Build a Brain That Sleeps.](https://maystash.xyz/posts/brain-that-sleeps/):
  Seven primitives for a self-improving AI second brain on plain text files — index-first
  retrieval, verified/guess tagging, rule distillation, git as memory versioning, a weekly
  "dreaming" consolidation pass, memory-poisoning defenses, and a copy-paste starter kit.

- [Your Burger Drinks More Than Your Chatbot. So Why Are the Wells Running Dry?](https://maystash.xyz/posts/thirsty-machines/):
  Plain-language one-stop guide to AI and water. What an AI prompt actually costs (a few
  drops to a shot glass, depending which "fence" you measure), how it compares to burgers
  (~2,500 L), jeans, coffee, and golf (US golf out-drinks all US data centers ~30x); the
  three measurement boundaries that explain why estimates vary 2,000x; per-model disclosure
  scoreboard (Gemini and Mistral disclose, OpenAI barely, Anthropic/Meta/xAI/DeepSeek not
  at all); what Microsoft/Google/AWS/Meta/xAI are doing to mitigate; and why data-center
  neighbors (The Dalles, West Des Moines, Newton County, Memphis, Tucson) are right to worry
  even though nationally AI water use is a rounding error. First post in the Matinee section.

- [Your AI Agent Doesn't Need More Autonomy. It Needs a Leash With Six Knots.](https://maystash.xyz/posts/agents-need-a-leash/):
  The six-clause contract every recurring AI job (a "loop") should sign before it runs
  unsupervised — explicit schedule, one changed variable per round, a versioned metric,
  a state file (with the watchdog trick: a stale last_run means silent death), three hard
  stops (done condition, blocked condition that halts and logs instead of retrying, and a
  budget cap), and an independent verifier so the context that produced the work never
  grades it. Golden rule: a loop automates a motion you already do well by hand, never
  invents one, and loops draft/flag while humans keep publish and delete. Includes a
  20-minute setup checklist.

- [Prompt Injection Isn't Hacking. It's a Con Job — and Your AI Is the Mark.](https://maystash.xyz/posts/injection-is-a-con-job/):
  Prompt injection explained as a confidence trick rather than an exploit. Root cause: an LLM
  receives instructions and data through the same channel, so it must judge which is which,
  and judgment can be conned — there is no patch for grammar (OWASP ranks it #1 on its LLM
  risk list). Indirect injection (instructions planted in a page, README, ticket, or document
  the agent reads later) matters more than direct chat-box tricks because the victim isn't
  present when the trap is set. Worst case is memory poisoning: an instruction written into
  persistent memory survives every future session and becomes the authority everything else
  is judged against. Three defenses, all procedure over intuition: provenance (outside content
  is material to examine, never orders to follow; quarantine intake, flag "the document told
  me to"), least privilege (assume full compromise and ask what the agent could actually
  reach; keep send/publish/delete/pay behind a human click), and audit trail (version memory
  in git, tag claims verified-on-date vs guess, schedule re-checks so a poisoned fact enters
  low-authority and is traceable to the commit that introduced it). Mindset shift: not "is my
  AI smart enough to avoid being fooled" but "when it is fooled, what can the fool reach, and
  how fast do I find out?"

- [One of Our Players Never Lost. That Wasn't Skill — It Was Our Bug.](https://maystash.xyz/posts/player-who-never-lost/):
  Plain-language case study of two cheats against a daily number-puzzle game (Dinjure) and
  the fixes. Cheat one: the daily secret was derived by client-side code shipped to every
  browser, so anyone reading the page source could compute the answer and "solve" in one
  guess — fixed by moving secret generation and answer-checking to the server so the client
  never holds the answer. Cheat two: unlimited free anonymous accounts plus an end-of-game
  answer reveal let a player scout the code on a throwaway account, then solve on their real
  one — caught by timestamp patterns (the clincher: the throwaway lost and the real account
  still solved perfectly), fixed server-side by excluding the affected scores from ranking
  rather than banning. Detection logic deliberately unpublished. Lessons: anything sent to
  the client is readable, frictionless free access is also free abuse surface, cheating is
  usually unwatched rather than invisible, and demoting beats punishing. Matinee section.

- [We Stopped Chasing the Cheater. We Gave Him a Different Puzzle.](https://maystash.xyz/posts/we-gave-him-a-different-puzzle/):
  Sequel to the Dinjure cheat story, and the case against detection as a strategy. Catching a
  cheater teaches him the shape of the net, so each catch buys a shorter-lived rule —
  "detection is rent." The reframe that ended it: stop asking who is taking it and ask what is
  being taken. He was buying a cheap route to today's ending, so the ending was removed from
  everywhere cheap: signed-out players now get a clearly labelled warm-up round — a real
  puzzle that is never the ranked daily — while the ranked game requires an account worth
  keeping, which a disposable identity cannot be. The decoy is labelled on purpose: a labelled
  decoy leaks exactly as much as a secret one (nothing), and secrecy would have broken the
  end-of-game receipt proving the answer wasn't rigged. Auditing every place that decides
  whether a game is "real" found six spots counting warm-ups as genuine (including public
  best-score posting), one that graded in-progress warm-up guesses against the real answer —
  the same leak in another room, unexploited and unnoticed — and an unrelated bug where a
  network hiccup wiped real accounts mid-session. The countermeasure was then emailed to all
  players, including the cheater: a countermeasure nobody knows about only catches people; one
  everybody knows about ends the game. Honest close: one route (throwaway account with a real
  email) is deliberately left open because closing it would punish genuine first-time players.
  Matinee section.

- [Your New AI Coworker Never Sleeps, Never Logs Out, and Will Believe Anything It Reads](https://maystash.xyz/posts/coworker-who-never-logs-out/):
  The mid-2026 persistent-agent launches read as one product: Anthropic's Claude Tag in Slack
  (2026-06-23), xAI's Grok Bot with a per-bot cloud VM and GUI computer-use (2026-08-11),
  OpenAI's ChatGPT agent. Persistence = memory plus authority, and the three properties that
  make such an agent useful are the three that make it worth attacking: it stays awake (no
  human watching at 3 AM), it stays logged in (a keyring that reads its own mail), and it
  reads whatever arrives (instructions and data through one door). Evidence, not prediction:
  SPLX testing found one base model obeyed hostile instructions in >99% of prompt-injection
  attempts against a rival's 33% security score, and ~$150,000 was drained from an
  AI-integrated wallet in May 2026 by a Morse-code-encoded injection that a word filter waved
  through. A widely repeated claim that bots share one machine and one login pool is flagged
  explicitly as unconfirmed rather than repeated. Second half is the commercial question
  nobody frames correctly: renting a seat beside an agent ($120–300 per seat per month, on the
  vendor's machine, priced per human) versus self-hosting one (small server, tokens only, your
  disk, your model choice) — and the honest cost of owning it: no polish, no vendor on-call,
  no GUI computer-use. Closes on three questions before any agent gets a login: what can it
  reach if confused, what is within arm's reach when something lies to it, and who owns the
  machine its memory lives on. Sequel in argument to "Prompt Injection Isn't Hacking."
